outline.chapter_title: Chapter 1: Case Context and Procedural History
outline.description: The petitioners in *Jimenez v. Bondi* are Wilson Leonardo Canon Jimenez, his wife Angelica Parada Duarte, and their two minor sons. Natives and citizens of Colombia, the family resided in Bogota prior to their departure for the United States in December 2022. Their eligibility for asylum hinges significantly on their background and public profile within their home country. Collectively, the family has been active members of the Colombian Liberal Party since 2012. This political affiliation placed them directly in opposition to the ruling party during the 2022 presidential election cycle. Specifically, they supported Federico Gutierrez, a candidate running against President Gustavo Petro. Their activism was not passive; they engaged in door-to-door canvassing to solicit votes for Gutierrez

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 2: Standards of Review and Legal Framework for Asylum
outline.description: When a law student first encounters an immigration appeal like *Jimenez v. Bondi*, the sheer volume of factual detail regarding threats, property disputes, and family dynamics can obscure the specific legal questions the court must answer. Before diving into the facts of the Jimenez family's ordeal, it is essential to understand the "lens" through which the Tenth Circuit viewed their case. This chapter establishes the foundational legal framework governing asylum claims and explains the highly deferential standard of review that governs appellate decisions in this field. Understanding these mechanics is crucial because, as the court's opinion reveals, even sympathetic factual narratives can fail to meet strict statutory thresholds if they do not align with these specific legal definitions

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 3: Analyzing Past Persecution – Severity and Cumulative Harm
outline.description: In the realm of asylum law, the threshold for establishing "past persecution" serves as a critical gateway to eligibility. As outlined in *Jimenez v. Bondi*, the definition of persecution remains fluid within the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), requiring courts to determine whether specific acts constitute "infliction of suffering or harm... regarded as offensive." However, the Tenth Circuit emphasizes that this standard demands more than mere restrictions on life or liberty; it requires a level of severity that transcends simple harassment.
